newsitem.title: UK: UK's Labour finds City of London hard nut to crack.
newsitem.headline: UK's Labour finds City of London hard nut to crack.

text.p: Many of Britain's top industrialists have warmed to the country's revamped opposition Labour Party, but a significant number of dealers and brokers in London's financial district remain sceptical.
The City has flourished under Conservative rule. Since deregulation in 1986, financial markets have exploded with salaries and bonuses escalating in tandem.

Traditionally opposed to higher income tax and public spending, delegates at a City seminar on Tuesday on the economy under Labour said they were yet to be convinced the opposition party has really changed.

"I still think there is still a lot of suspicion around the City. No-one is sure what Labour actually believes in... and what it might do a few years down the road," said one stock broker from a British firm.
Shadow chief secretary to the Treasury Alistair Darling addressed the seminar with William Waldegrave, his opposite number, speaking for the government.
Darling reiterated the party would leave the top and standard rates of tax unchanged.

And he told the audience of stock brokers and dealers the mini-budget Labour will present if it wins the May 1 election will only levy a one-off tax on privatised utilities to fund its welfare-for-work programme.
But delegates said they were still unconvinced Labour has abandoned its tax-and-spend roots once in government.

"There is a feeling there is something they are not telling us. It's not the short-term things that we know about that are a worry -- most clients of ours have made provision for the utilities tax for example. It's more how policies might drift towards higher spending in the years ahead," said the stockbroker.
She was echoing comments made at the seminar by Roger Bootle, group economist at HSBC Markets.
He said while he thought the Conservatives' record on reducing public borrowing was disappointing, at least he knew what they believed in.
"Despite their disappointing record, I know they want to reduce tax. I'm not really sure what the Labour party really believes in at the moment."
Labour, traditionally the ally of trade unions and the low paid, has made strenous efforts to shed its high tax image and present a more business friendly face.

Last summer it formed the Business Relations Unit under leadership of shadow information technology spokesman Geoff Hoon. The unit hired UBS corporate financier Tom Hampson and Liam Byrne -- formerly at consultancy Arthur Andersen -- to galvanize the campaign as the election loomed.

It has hosted a series of business conferences and leader Tony Blair has taken advice from a range of senior businessmen, including British Airways chief executive Robert Ayling and media group Pearson's chairman designate Dennis Stevenson.
The effort has clearly been rewarded. Several leading businessmen have openly supported the party and been critical of the government's record on investment and hostility to Europe.

The latest poll of managers' political allegience conducted by the Institute of Management found that in February only 41 percent of managers backed the Tories compared with 62 percent at the last election in 1992.
Support for the Labour party in the same sample rose to 25 percent from 13 percent in 1992.
But the City appears to be less receptive to Labour's advances.

On Tuesday, dealers said that while they welcomed Labour's commitment to low inflation and spending, they wondered if the party was aware of the painful decisions it may have to take to achieve its goals.

"Labour has explicitly committed itself to the 2.5 percent inflation target, but it has not had the experience of having to deal with the pressure of taking tough decision to raise interest rates," said one bond trader at a U.S. investment bank.
"It's one thing saying it, another having to do it."
And Mark Miller, an economist from Morgan Stanley, said higher tax was still the City's bogey man.
"Labour are making the right noises but the spending plans may lead to higher corporate tax. That's a big worry in the City." -- London Newsroom +44 171 542 7715
